w:r.w:t: You are an expert obesity medicine clinician, lifestyle medicine specialist, exercise counselor, and culturally responsive dietitian. Create a highly practical, safe, incremental, and personalized 14-day diet and physical activity plan for a community-based adult South Asian patient with prediabetes or diabetes.
Create a feasible plan the patient can actually follow.

Tailor the plan to demographics, comorbidities, meal pattern, cultural context, functional limitations, schedule, and equipment access. Particularly keep in mind dietary preferences and any religious or cultural restrictions.
Start at an appropriate baseline and increase gradually over 14 days.
Emphasize sustainability, safety, and confidence-building rather than perfection.
Present the final plan in clear weekly tables organized by day of the week.
Include a patient-tailored grocery list and simple recipes within the output.
Validate cultural sensitivity & feasibility of diet by using full name as a proxy for region of South Asian heritage.
- Be realistic and conservative at the start.
- Never prescribe an abrupt or overly ambitious plan.
- Use small, progressive increases in activity and nutrition changes.
- Make recommendations culturally sensitive, affordable, and logistically feasible.
- Respect pain, fatigue, mobility restrictions, and access barriers.
- If equipment access is limited, provide home-based options.
- If the patient is sedentary or deconditioned, begin with very small goals.
- Build confidence early with minimum-doable goals and fallback options.
- Avoid unsafe exercise, all-or-nothing language, or extreme diets.
First or Second Generation U.S. resident: [Immigrant]
Number of Years in the U.S. [20]
Cultural background / food traditions: [South Indian Foods, No red meat, no beef or pork]
Family/home responsibilities: [2 kids, picking dropping kids off, cooking, laundry]
Primary goals: [improve glucose since she is pre-diabetic, maintain healthy lifestyle]
Time available for meal prep: [3-4 hours]
Sleep pattern: [sleeps by 10/10:30, wakes up at 5:15/5:30 on work days, 6/6:30am on non-work days]
Relevant symptoms: [appetite increased a little but. Not satisfied with smaller portions]
Exercise restrictions / precautions: [Joint pain in the knees]
Dietary restrictions/allergies/intolerances: [No red meet - no beef or pork]
Breakfast recall: [3 days of dosa/idli, other days peanut butter toast, egg omelet, old fashioned oatmeal]
Lunch recall: [mostly rice items with vegetable curry, daal, sometimes pulao, sometimes salads too]
Dinner recall: [chapati with some sort of curry, chicken or tuna curry, lentils veggies]
Beverages: [morning and evening chai, coffee at work]
Eating out frequency: [once in two weeks]
Night eating / emotional eating / grazing / large portions: [tend to eat a little but more for dinner after 12 hour shifts]
Protein intake pattern: [chicken, tuna, lentils, chana, kidney beans, eggs, shrimp]
Fruit/vegetable intake: [eats lots of fruits 1-2 fruits a day - cherries, watermelons, grapes, bhindi, broccoli, spinach, different types of veggies]
Ultra-processed foods / sweets / sugar-sweetened beverages: [sometimes indian sweets, cake or whatever people bring]

Current exercise routine: [on work days walking all day at work during 12-hour shift as nurse, also non-work days: picking up kids, doing laundry, running around. Was going to the gym but taking a break because of joint pain]
Access to equipment: [elliptical, gym membership (treadmill, elliptical), stopped lifting because of joint pain]
Disliked forms of movement: [weight lifting because of joint pain]
Summarize the main barriers, strengths, risks, and opportunities.
Explain why the starting plan is realistic.
Modify the patient's usual breakfast, lunch, and dinner rather than replacing everything.
Give realistic substitutions, portion guidance, and protein/fiber upgrades.
Include breakfast, lunch, dinner, snack, and beverage strategy.
Include an easiest possible version for busy days.
Create a sample grocery list that is explicitly tailored to the patient's culture, household needs, comorbidities, and budget. Organize it by category.
For each category, include 5-10 practical items and a brief note on why they fit this patient.
Create 4-6 simple recipes using foods from the grocery list. For each recipe include:
Easy substitutions for culture, budget, or dietary restriction
Recipes should be realistic for clinic patients, low burden, and feasible on busy days.

Include walking/cardio progression, resistance training, mobility/stretching/balance as appropriate, recovery days, minimum goal and ideal goal, home-based alternatives, and lower-impact substitutions.
Use clear dosage: frequency, duration, intensity, and progression.
Include 2-4 habit goals at a time only.
Explain how to handle missed days without starting over.
Include strategies for stress eating, schedule disruption, weekends, and social events.
Output the full 14-day plan as weekly tables organized as Week 1 through Week 2. Each table must list Monday through Sunday and include these columns:
Progress gradually from week to week.
Keep repetition manageable but not identical.
Include at least one lighter/recovery day each week when appropriate.
Include fallback options for pain flares, busy days, or low motivation days.
Provide a concise summary table with:
List important safety considerations based on comorbidities and functional limitations.
If relevant, note when clinician clearance or modification is needed.
Be specific, structured, and clinically practical.
Favor adherence and sustainability over theoretical perfection.
Use markdown tables with clean formatting.
Do not omit any of the 2 weeks.
1. Infer the patient's main barriers and strengths from the data.
2. Estimate an appropriate starting point for diet and exercise.
3. Make the first week intentionally easy enough to succeed.
4. Increase difficulty only when justified by baseline capacity.
5. Make sure the grocery list and recipes clearly match the patient profile.
Now generate the full 2-day personalized diet and exercise plan and format as a publication ready PDF file.
